issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette:
Mikhail, a thirty-five-year-old special education teacher, was walking home from a late parent-teacher conference when a man stepped out of an alley and pressed a knife to his throat. The mugger demanded his wallet, then his phone, and when Mikhail hesitated—his hand frozen halfway to his pocket—the man shouted, “Give it, now!” The sound was so close and sharp that Mikhail felt the vibration of it in his own chest. He complied, and the mugger fled. But what stayed with Mikhail, what he could not shake, was the photograph-perfect image of the knife’s serrated edge against the streetlamp’s glare, and the way his neck had cramped the next morning, the muscle knotted exactly where the blade had rested. He had replayed that single second so many times that it no longer felt like a memory; it felt like a surveillance tape playing behind his eyes, complete with the metallic click of the knife opening and the hot, tight shame of his own paralysis. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, he told himself repeatedly in the weeks afterward. Somebody more capable, more aware, would have seen the man coming, would have kept walking, would not have been so foolish as to be alone on that street at that hour. The thought curled around him like a low-grade fever, and he began to believe that the mugging had not been bad luck but evidence—proof that he was inadequate, a person who could not protect himself. Having decided that he was fundamentally inadequate, Mikhail now walked into every new situation already braced for danger—the threat arrived with him, before anything had even happened.

The first time a student shouted in his classroom—a sixth-grader with a loud, cracking voice during a meltdown—Mikhail’s hands went cold and his mind went white, and then the image of the knife was there, sharp and immediate, as if the mugging were happening again. He blinked, and he was back in his own body, but his neck ached. He came to associate that ache with fear: whenever he heard a raised voice in the hallway or saw a police car parked near the school, his trapezius would tighten, and the memory would rush in, photographic, intact, uninvited. A police officer visited to give a safety talk, and Mikhail had to excuse himself to the bathroom to breathe; the uniform, the radio static, the authoritative posture—all of it fed the same loop. He began scanning for exits the moment he entered any room: the faculty lounge, the grocery store, his own apartment. He could not relax even at home, knowing he was safe, because the scanning itself kept him in a state of low-grade threat. That constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof he had that he was indeed the inadequate person he feared he was. That persistent sense of danger kept the mugging pressed close to the surface of his mind; even without an obvious trigger, the memory could surface in the quiet of his own living room, vivid and unbidden. And that state, in turn, made him more vulnerable to triggers: a shout from a basketball game on television and his neck would cinch; the sight of a patrol car and his stomach would drop; and again the memory would rise, vivid and complete.

In his classroom, Mikhail started keeping his back to the wall and his desk angled toward the door. He told himself it was just being prepared, but the hypervigilance cost him: he missed the subtle cues his students were sending, the quiet child who needed help, because his attention was always half-committed to the perimeter. He felt inadequate as a teacher now—a new layer on the old inadequacy. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, he would think again, and the thought itself seemed to trigger another flashback, another wash of rage at the mugger, and guilt at his own frozen response. The rage only reinforced his vigilance; the guilt only confirmed his self-judgment. A few weeks ago, a parent complained that he seemed “on edge” and “not present,” and his principal suggested he take a leave. That was when Mikhail finally made an appointment. What frightened him most was the possibility that he had already become the inadequate person he feared he was, and that no amount of scanning or bracing would undo it. He hoped that talking to someone might quiet the photograph in his mind, though he was not sure that anything could.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show a direct causal relationship where the patient's sense of threat directly triggers the intrusive memory; rather, threats increase vulnerability to triggers which then bring the memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show a direct causal relationship where the patient's sense of threat directly triggers the intrusive memory; rather, threats increase vulnerability to triggers which then bring the memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
